title: Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB (1998)
shortTitle: Allentown Mack Sales & Service, Inc. v. NLRB (1998)
summary: An agency must actually apply the legal standard it announces, and a reviewing court measures the agency's factfinding against that announced standard, so the Board's finding that an employer lacked a good faith reasonable doubt of union support was unsupported by substantial evidence.
notes:
Key line: "An agency should not be able to impede judicial review, and indeed even political oversight, by disguising its policymaking as factfinding." (Scalia, J.)

Citation: 522 U.S. 359 (1998).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Allentown Mack Sales and Service, Inc., a truck dealership in Allentown, Pennsylvania, formed by former managers of a Mack Trucks factory branch who bought its assets. The respondent was the National Labor Relations Board, which had found the company guilty of an unfair labor practice for polling its employees about union support. The union involved was Local Lodge 724 of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, which had represented the service and parts employees of the Mack branch. The Chamber of Commerce, the American Trucking Associations and the Labor Policy Association filed briefs for the company; the AFL-CIO supported the Board.
sections.Material Facts: Mack Trucks announced in May 1990 that it would sell its Allentown branch. Allentown Mack bought the business on December 20, 1990, and between December 21, 1990, and January 1, 1991, hired 32 of the 45 former Mack employees. During the sale, eight employees made statements in job interviews suggesting they no longer wanted the union. Ron Mohr, a union shop steward and bargaining committee member, told a manager that the employees did not want a union and that the union would lose a vote at a new company. Kermit Bloch, a night shift mechanic, said the entire night shift of five or six employees did not want the union. On January 2, 1991, Local 724 demanded recognition. Allentown refused by letter of January 25, citing a good faith doubt, and announced a secret ballot poll. The poll was held on February 8, 1991; the union lost 19 to 13 and filed an unfair labor practice charge.
sections.Procedural History: An administrative law judge found Allentown a successor employer that inherited a presumption of continuing majority support, found the poll procedurally proper under Struksnes Construction Co., but held it violated sections 8(a)(1) and 8(a)(5) of the National Labor Relations Act because Allentown lacked an objective reasonable doubt of majority status. The Board adopted the findings, 316 N.L.R.B. 1199 (1995), and ordered Allentown to recognize and bargain with the union. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit enforced the order over a dissent, 83 F.3d 1483 (1996). The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 520 U.S. 1103 (1997), heard argument on October 15, 1997, and on January 26, 1998, reversed and remanded with instructions to deny enforcement.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, whether the Board's rule that an employer may poll employees about union support only when it already has a good faith reasonable doubt of the union's majority status, the same showing required to withdraw recognition outright, is rational and consistent with the Act, or is arbitrary because it makes polling legally pointless. Second, whether the Board's finding that Allentown lacked such a doubt was supported by substantial evidence on the record as a whole, including whether the Board could discount probative circumstantial evidence based on its past practice of demanding express repudiation by a majority of employees.
sections.Holding: The Court held, by a vote of 5 to 4 in Part II, that the Board's unitary standard for polling, withdrawal of recognition and Board conducted elections is facially rational and consistent with the Act, because an employer may have reasons to poll other than insulating a withdrawal of recognition and the Board could rationally split the difference between higher and lower thresholds. It held, by a different 5 to 4 vote in Parts III and IV, that the Board's finding that Allentown lacked a good faith reasonable doubt was not supported by substantial evidence. Doubt means uncertainty, not disbelief; given seven confirmed disavowals among 32 employees plus the statements of Mohr and Bloch, no reasonable factfinder could avoid the conclusion that Allentown was reasonably uncertain about majority support.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Scalia wrote that substantial evidence review asks whether a reasonable jury could have reached the Board's conclusion. The Board's finding rested on a refusal to credit probative circumstantial evidence and on evidentiary demands beyond the standard it purported to apply. The ALJ discounted Bloch's and Mohr's statements because they did not explain how they knew their coworkers' views, when the question was the employer's reasonable uncertainty rather than the fact of disaffection, and the Board's refusal to rely on Mohr because he spoke of Mack's workforce was irrational when the union's own claim rested on the presumption that the successor's workforce shared its predecessor's views. Accepting seven disavowals, the remaining 25 employees would have had to favor the union by 17 to 8. The Court then addressed the argument that the Board had consistently required a strict head count in earlier cases. The APA establishes a scheme of reasoned decisionmaking, and the process by which an agency reaches a result must be logical and rational. An agency may adopt higher standards of proof or evidentiary presumptions openly, by rule or explicit announcement in adjudication, subject to review for reasonableness. But it may not leave one standard formally in place while consistently applying another, because that prevents consistent application by ALJs, frustrates judicial review, and disguises policymaking as factfinding. Reviewing courts take the announced standards to mean what they say and conduct substantial evidence review on that basis.

topics.lrs-n-substantial-evidence: The Court upheld the legal policy but found the Board ignored evidence relevant under its own standard.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: Scalia's opinion insists that an agency actually apply the standard it announces rather than a covert stricter one, a reasoned-decisionmaking point beyond the substantial-evidence quantum.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Scalia delivered the opinion of the Court in full only as to Part I. Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justices O'Connor, Kennedy and Thomas, joined Parts III and IV but dissented from Part II, arguing that the Board's polling standard is irrational because it forbids polling except when a poll has almost no practical value and requires the employer to obtain information it is barred from gathering by the most effective means. Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg, joined Parts I and II but dissented from Parts III and IV, arguing that the substantial evidence question was not presented, that the Court ignored Universal Camera's limit on Supreme Court intervention in such review, and that the Court rewrote the Board's technical standard of objective reasonable doubt into an ordinary jury standard without deferring to the Board's evidentiary presumptions.
